overview: New Zealand is an island country in the south-west Pacific, made up mainly of the North Island and the South Island. Its capital is Wellington and its largest city is Auckland. Māori settled the islands about 700 years ago, and New Zealand became a British colony in 1840 after the Treaty of Waitangi. Most people speak English, and Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are official languages.

geography.text: New Zealand is long and mountainous. The Southern Alps run down the South Island, with glaciers, lakes and fjords such as Milford Sound. The North Island has volcanoes, geysers and hot springs, especially around Rotorua and Lake Taupō. Because the islands were isolated for so long, they have unique wildlife, including the flightless kiwi.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Mild and wet, with snow in the Southern Alps.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Kiwi birds, kea parrots and tuatara, a reptile from the age of dinosaurs.

history.text: Polynesian voyagers, the ancestors of the Māori, settled New Zealand about 700 years ago, making it one of the last large landmasses on Earth to be settled by people. The Dutch explorer Abel Tasman reached it in 1642, and James Cook mapped it in 1769. The Treaty of Waitangi was signed between Māori chiefs and the British Crown in 1840. In 1893 New Zealand became the first country where women could vote in national elections.

events.title: Tasman arrives
events.text: Abel Tasman is the first European known to reach New Zealand.

events.title: Treaty of Waitangi
events.text: Māori chiefs and the British Crown sign a founding treaty.

events.title: Votes for women
events.text: New Zealand is the first country to give women the vote in national elections.

events.title: Everest climbed
events.text: New Zealander Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reach the summit of Everest.

government.text: New Zealand is a constitutional monarchy. The British monarch is head of state, represented by a Governor-General. The Prime Minister leads the government with the support of Parliament, which has a single chamber. Some seats are reserved for Māori voters. New Zealand has no single written constitution.

economy.text: New Zealand exports dairy products, meat, wood, fruit such as kiwifruit, and wine. Tourism is big, and the film industry grew after the Lord of the Rings films were shot there. Most of its electricity comes from renewable sources.

culture.text: Māori culture is central to New Zealand's identity. Te reo Māori is an official language, and many places have Māori names. The haka, a Māori ceremonial dance, is performed at important events. The country's landscapes became famous worldwide as Middle-earth in the Lord of the Rings films.

items.title: The haka
items.text: A Māori ceremonial dance, performed before All Blacks matches.

items.title: Middle-earth
items.text: The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit films were shot in New Zealand.

items.title: Kiwi
items.text: A flightless bird and the nickname for New Zealanders.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Hāngī, food cooked in an earth oven, and pavlova.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Māori carving, tattoo (tā moko) and kapa haka performance.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: Waitangi Day, 6 February, marks the 1840 treaty.

sport.text: Rugby union is the national sport, and the All Blacks are one of the most successful teams in any sport, with three Rugby World Cup wins. New Zealand also excels in sailing, rowing and netball, and hosted the 2023 Women's World Cup with Australia.

items.title: America's Cup
items.text: New Zealand has won the famous sailing trophy several times.

items.title: Edmund Hillary
items.text: Climbed Everest in 1953 with Tenzing Norgay.

didYouKnow: New Zealand was the first country where women could vote in national elections, in 1893.
There are about five sheep for every person in New Zealand.

keyPeople.text: Split the atom and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
